THE GATHERING STORM

Rain had been falling since morning, and the little town at the foot of
the pass had drawn its shutters against it. Nobody expected a visitor.

By evening the road was a river of mud, and still the lamps of the inn
burned steadily, as they had for a hundred winters before this one.

A COLD ARRIVAL

The stranger came on foot, which no one did in such weather, and asked
for a room without once lowering the collar that hid half of his face.

The innkeeper, who had learned long ago not to ask questions of paying
guests, gave him the key to the room above the kitchen and said nothing.

THE MORNING AFTER

When the sun finally returned it found the stranger already gone, the
key left on the sill, and a single gold coin resting beside it.

No one in the town ever learned his name, but the coin bought bread for
a week, and the story of the night lasted a great deal longer than that.
